questions.stem: What happens to electrons during ionic bond formation?

options.text: A metal transfers electrons to a non-metal
options.explanation: Loss leaves the metal a cation; gain leaves the non-metal an anion.

options.text: Electrons are shared equally between the two atoms
options.explanation: Sharing defines covalent bonding instead.

options.text: Electrons are destroyed to neutralise both atoms
options.explanation: Electrons are conserved and transferred, never destroyed.

options.text: Electrons are borrowed temporarily and returned
options.explanation: The transfer is permanent in the compound formed.

questions.stem: Which ion configuration does a chloride ion share?

options.text: No noble gas - chloride keeps [2,8,7]
options.explanation: The gained electron completes the octet.

options.text: Argon, at [2,8,8]
options.explanation: Chlorine gains one electron onto [2,8,7], reaching argon's arrangement.

options.text: Neon, at [2,8]
options.explanation: That is a period-2 configuration, one shell short.

options.text: Krypton, at [2,8,18,8]
options.explanation: Chloride's three shells stop at 18 electrons.

questions.stem: A potassium ion has the same electronic configuration as

options.text: Krypton, at [2,8,18,8]
options.explanation: K+ stops at eighteen electrons across three shells.

options.text: Helium, at [2]
options.explanation: Helium's two-electron shell is far smaller.

options.text: Argon, written [2,8,8]+
options.explanation: K loses its single outer electron from [2,8,8,1].

options.text: Calcium, at [2,8,8,2]
options.explanation: Calcium carries an extra shell and two more protons.

questions.stem: Why do ionic compounds have high melting points?

options.text: Covalent bonds inside molecules resist heat
options.explanation: Ionic compounds contain no molecular covalent bonds.

options.text: Their ions spin faster at higher temperature
options.explanation: Spin is not part of the melting argument.

options.text: Electrons flow and generate heat resistance
options.explanation: Solid ionic compounds do not conduct at all.

options.text: Large energy is needed to overcome the strong electrostatic attractions running through the lattice
options.explanation: Every ion grips several oppositely charged neighbours at once.

questions.stem: Why is the final ionic crystal always electrically neutral?

options.text: Positive charges cancel negative charges exactly across the repeating pattern
options.explanation: The lattice packs ions in proportions that balance total charge to zero.

options.text: Electrons escape the crystal until it is neutral
options.explanation: Electrons stay with their new anions.

options.text: Neutrons in the nuclei offset the ionic charges
options.explanation: Neutrons carry no charge and cannot cancel anything.

options.text: The metal keeps some electrons back
options.explanation: The transfer is complete for the formula adopted.

questions.stem: State what a metal atom becomes and what a non-metal atom becomes in ionic bond formation.
questions.modelAnswer: The metal atom loses electrons and becomes a positively charged cation; the non-metal atom gains electrons and becomes a negatively charged anion.

questions.stem: State the noble gas whose configuration both K+ and Cl- adopt.
questions.modelAnswer: Both potassium ions and chloride ions carry argon's configuration, [2,8,8].

questions.stem: Explain why ionic attraction is called non-directional whereas covalent bonding is not.
questions.modelAnswer: A cation attracts every surrounding anion equally from any approach angle, so the bond has no preferred heading; a covalent bond exists only along the axis between the two nuclei sharing the pair.

questions.stem: Identify the ion formed when magnesium loses its two outer electrons and give its noble-gas-matched configuration.
questions.modelAnswer: Magnesium forms Mg2+, matching neon's configuration [2,8] after the third shell is emptied.

questions.stem: Which electrons appear in a dot-and-cross diagram?

options.text: Only the newly transferred electrons
options.explanation: The remaining outer electrons of both ions are also shown.

options.text: Only the outer-shell electrons
options.explanation: Inner shells stay undrawn by convention.

options.text: Every electron the atoms own
options.explanation: Inner-shell electrons are omitted to keep the picture readable.

options.text: Only the electrons the metal loses
options.explanation: The non-metal's electrons are drawn too, as dots or crosses.

questions.stem: Where is an ion's charge written on a dot-and-cross diagram?

options.text: Inside the bracket beside the nucleus
options.explanation: The charge sits outside the brackets.

options.text: Above the whole diagram as a caption
options.explanation: Each ion carries its own corner charge.

options.text: At the top right-hand corner outside the bracket
options.explanation: The convention places the magnitude and sign there.

options.text: At the bottom left of the bracket
options.explanation: The convention fixes the top right.

questions.stem: Why do square brackets wrap each ion in the diagram?

options.text: To mark atoms that failed to react
options.explanation: Brackets wrap every ionic species.

options.text: To double the electron count visually
options.explanation: Brackets change no electron count.

options.text: To distinguish metals from non-metals
options.explanation: Both ion types receive brackets.

options.text: To show the charge is spread evenly over the whole ion
options.explanation: The brackets collect the ion into one unit carrying the corner charge.

questions.stem: A lithium atom transfers its outer electron to a fluorine atom. In the diagram, the transferred electron is drawn as

options.text: a cross inside fluorine's bracketed shell
options.explanation: Crosses track the donor lithium's electrons wherever they end up.

options.text: a dot inside lithium's bracketed shell
options.explanation: The electron has left lithium; it is drawn at its new home.

options.text: a dot and a cross side by side
options.explanation: Each electron carries exactly one origin symbol.

options.text: an open circle outside both shells
options.explanation: No third symbol exists in the convention.

questions.stem: What must a finished ionic dot-and-cross diagram show about both ions?

options.text: Inner shells drawn for comparison
options.explanation: Inner shells stay off the page.

options.text: Both ions reach full outer shells
options.explanation: The transfer completes the octets of both species.

options.text: Both ions keep partially filled shells
options.explanation: Full shells are the point of the transfer.

options.text: The metal ion larger than the non-metal ion
options.explanation: Cations shrink; diagrams do not even fix sizes to scale.

questions.stem: State the three drawing conventions of dot-and-cross diagrams.
questions.modelAnswer: Only outer electrons appear; brackets enclose each ion to spread its charge evenly; the charge sits at the top right of the bracketed ion.

questions.stem: Describe what electron transfer achieves for both atoms in an ionic compound.
questions.modelAnswer: The metal atom loses its outer electrons and the non-metal gains them, leaving both ions with noble gas configurations.

questions.stem: Explain why only outer-shell electrons need to be drawn in these diagrams.
questions.modelAnswer: Bonding and charge are decided entirely by the valence shell: inner electrons neither transfer nor affect the attraction, so drawing them adds clutter without information.

questions.stem: Draw-in-words the dot-and-cross description of sodium chloride formation from Na and Cl atoms.
questions.modelAnswer: Sodium's single outer electron (a cross) is transferred into chlorine's outer shell (dots); the diagram shows [Na]+ with an empty outer shell and [Cl]- with eight outer electrons, both bracketed with corner charges.

questions.stem: Why does calcium fluoride contain two fluoride ions per calcium ion?

options.text: Calcium donates two electrons to each fluorine
options.explanation: Each fluorine accepts only one electron; the calcium's two electrons go to two different atoms.

options.text: The lattice has twice as many sites for anions
options.explanation: Site counts follow the charge ratio, not the reverse.

options.text: Each F- carries one negative charge, so two are needed to cancel Ca2+
options.explanation: Charge neutrality forces the 1:2 ratio.

options.text: Fluorine atoms are twice as heavy
options.explanation: Mass plays no role in charge balancing.

questions.stem: What charge does an aluminium ion carry, and how many electrons did it lose?

options.text: 2+, having lost two outer electrons
options.explanation: That describes a group 2 metal such as magnesium.

options.text: 3-, having gained three electrons
options.explanation: Metals lose electrons; gains make anions.

options.text: 1+, having lost one electron
options.explanation: Aluminium's valence shell holds three electrons.

options.text: 3+, having lost three outer electrons
options.explanation: Group 3 metal aluminium empties its valence shell.

questions.stem: Which formula correctly balances Al3+ against O2-?

options.text: Al2O3, two aluminium ions to three oxide ions
options.explanation: 2 x (+3) + 3 x (-2) = 0 certifies neutrality.

options.text: AlO3, one aluminium to three oxide ions
options.explanation: That totals +3 - 6 = -3, not neutral.

options.text: Al3O2, three aluminium ions to two oxide ions
options.explanation: That totals +9 - 4 = +5.

options.text: AlO, one of each
options.explanation: That totals +3 - 2 = +1.

questions.stem: Lithium nitride contains three lithium ions per nitride ion. What charge does a nitride ion carry?

options.text: 3+, a positive nitrogen ion
options.explanation: Nitrogen is a non-metal; its ion is negative.

options.text: 3-, since three Li+ ions (each +1) cancel one N3-
options.explanation: 3(+1) + (-3) = 0 keeps Li3N neutral.

options.text: 1-, matching each lithium ion
options.explanation: One-to-one would leave the crystal neutral with LiN, but the formula is Li3N.

options.text: 2-, needing two lithium ions
options.explanation: Two cancellations leave one lithium charge unbalanced.

questions.stem: In the calcium fluoride lattice, what must hold for the crystal to be neutral?

options.text: Half the calcium ions are actually neutral atoms
options.explanation: All species are ions in the compound.

options.text: The fluorine ions share their extra electrons
options.explanation: The gained electrons stay with each fluoride ion.

options.text: Every Ca2+ is balanced by two nearby F- ions throughout the structure
options.explanation: The 1:2 ionic ratio repeats across the whole lattice, cancelling all charge.

options.text: Some electrons roam freely to even out charge
options.explanation: Ionic lattices have no delocalised electrons.

questions.stem: State the formula of calcium fluoride and the charges that produce it.
questions.modelAnswer: CaF2 forms from Ca2+ and F- ions: two singly charged fluoride ions balance one doubly charged calcium ion.

questions.stem: State the formulae of lithium nitride and aluminium oxide.
questions.modelAnswer: Lithium nitride is Li3N (three Li+ per N3-) and aluminium oxide is Al2O3 (two Al3+ per three O2-).

questions.stem: Explain why aluminium oxide cannot have the formula AlO.
questions.modelAnswer: AlO would carry +3 from aluminium against only -2 from one oxide ion, leaving a net +1 charge; neutrality requires the cross-multiplied 2:3 ratio of Al2O3.

questions.stem: Use the charge-balance rule to build the formula of calcium chloride, then state why it matches the calcium fluoride pattern.
questions.modelAnswer: Ca2+ meets two Cl- ions: 1 x (+2) + 2 x (-1) = 0, so the formula is CaCl2 - the same 1:2 ratio as CaF2 because both anions carry a single negative charge.
